title: RKC upgrade: monomial as type parameter, adaptive regularization
body:
**Breaking (v0.6.0)**

- `RKCMaterial{CM,K,DM,M}` / `RKCRMaterial{CM,K,DM,M}`: the monomial is now the last type parameter (`AbstractRKCMaterial{CM,C,M}`), read with `monomial(mat)`. The moment matrix in `rkc_weights!` has a compile-time size → 0 allocations, JET-clean for all monomials, the @test_broken perf items are real tests now.
- New epsilon keyword (default `1e-3`): adaptive per-singular-value floor via `invreg(M, ε)`. lambda/beta still select the legacy regularization; combining both is an error. Bit-identical to the exact inverse on intact families, only acts once a family is near rank-deficient.
- `log_material` for the RKC family prints the monomial and only the active regularization.
- `isolated_point` guard: a point whose family has no kinematic weight left (softening models) transmits no stress instead of 1/0, a no-op for bond-deleting models.

title: Constitutive-model state (`@cm_storage`)
body:
A constitutive model can now carry and integrate its own per-point / per-bond state:

- `Peridynamics.@cm_storage Model struct State … end` declares the state with the same
  field shapes as `@storage`; a material carries it via `cm_state::ConstitutiveState`
  (`CMaterial`, `RKCMaterial`, `BACMaterial` do)
- `first_piola_kirchhoff(model, storage, params, F, idx, Δt)` / `strain_energy_density(…, idx)`
  are the canonical signatures; stateless models keep the 4-arg form (bridged, zero cost)
- `is_history_dependent` / `supports_history_dependence` are checked when a `Job` is created
  (`HistoryDependenceError`); `NewtonKrylov` rejects history-dependent models
- `get_constitutive_model(mat)` accessor for every material family with a model

Part of the v0.6.0 extensibility rework, no behaviour change for existing models.

title: New storage declaration framework
body:
Replaces the `@pointfield`/`@lthfield`/`@htlfield` storage macros with declarative **field shapes** (`PointVector`, `BondTensor`, `DofVector`, …) and inheritable **field blocks** (`@storage_fields`, `@inherit`), so that a material storage is written as
```julia
@storage MyMaterial struct MyStorage
    @inherit VelocityVerletFields DynamicRelaxationFields NewtonKrylovFields
    @inherit BondFracFields
    my_field::PointScalar
end
```

### Core features
- shaped fields are allocated from the system and the solver, no `init_field` needed
- time solvers claim fields with `FullField`/`EmptyField` instead of allocating them
- the storage contract (material, damage model, solver) is checked when a Job is created
  (`StorageContractError`)
- generated storages are parametric in the float type and get an `Adapt.adapt_structure`
  method (new deps: `Adapt`, `Markdown`)
- all built-in materials, `TestMaterialImpl` and the tests are migrated, behaviour and
  performance are unchanged

Part of the extensibility rework for v0.6.0.

title: Make the `DynamicRelaxation` damping global and decomposition-independent
body:
Fixes #288.

The ADR damping coefficient is now the one global Rayleigh quotient over all degrees
of freedom of the body, for every data handler:

- `damping_terms(chunk, Δt)` computes the local partial sums of `cn1`/`cn2`,
- the partials are combined over all chunks (threads: one extra parallel pass per
  step) or all ranks (MPI: one `Allgather` of a 32-byte struct per step, combined in
  rank order so every rank computes the identical value),
- `finish_damping` applies the square root and clamping once.
  The multibody handler reduces per body, matching what a serial multibody run computes.

The partial sums are accumulated with **compensated summation** (`two_sum`) and carry
their compensation terms through the reduction. This matters: with plain summation the
reduced sums round differently for different chunkings (1 ulp), which the underdamped
dynamics amplify (~1e-5 rel), and with failure enabled a 1-ulp difference can break a
different set of bonds (~1e-2). With compensation, runs with 1/2/3/4 chunks are
**bitwise identical**, with and without fracture.

title: Overhaul of the testing suite
body:
Full overhauling of the testing suite.

## New Layout

| Directory | Contents | Tags | CI job |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unit/<dir>/` | unit tests mirroring `src/`: `unit/<dir>/test_<file>.jl` tests `src/<dir>/<file>.jl` | — | `test` |
| `materials/` | one item per property, looping `Fixtures.MATERIALS` (storage fields, force density invariants, stress/energy exports, the material interface) | — / `:slow` | `test` / `extras` |
| `simulation/` | the per-commit time loops: symmetry of every solver, uniform tension | `:simulation` | `test` |
| `mpi/` | three `mpiexec` runs (core paths, abort, threads comparison), scripts in `mpi/scripts/` | `:mpi` | `mpi` |
| `perf/` | allocation and type stability checks | `:perf` | `extras` |
| `quality/` | Aqua and the convention guards | `:lint` | `extras` |
| `verification/` | physics against closed forms and convergence rates | `:verification, :skipci` | never |
| `setup/` | the shared `@testmodule`s: `Fixtures` (materials table, bodies, chunks, condition functions, `rng()`) and `TestMaterialImpl` | | |

`test/runtests.jl` selects by `PERIDYNAMICS_TESTS` (`default`, `mpi`, `extras`, `all`); see
`.github/workflows/CI.yml`.

v3.0.0

:warning: Breaking Changes, and Migration Guide for v2 ⟶ v3

  1. v3 requires Node 24 (compared to v2, which required Node 20).
  2. The behavior of version: min has changed between v2 and v3.
    • In v2, version: min would resolve to the minimum major/minor/patch, e.g. 1.10.0.
    • In v3, version: min resolves to the minimum major/minor but the latest patch, e.g. 1.10.11.
    • If you specifically want the minimum major/minor/patch under v3, you should specify version: min-patch. Note: v3 also adds the alias version: min-minor, which is equivalent to version: min.
  3. v3 will throw an error if x86_64 Julia binaries are requested on Apple Silicon macOS. (Under v2, this was a warning.) Under v3, if you specifically want to run x86_64 Julia binaries on Apple Silicon (under Rosetta 2), you must now opt-in by specifying the force-arch: true input.

Other Changes

body:
The perturbation during the Newton-Krylov simulations is now adaptively calculated with the heuristic
```math
\varepsilon = \alpha_{\mathrm{user}} \cdot \sqrt[3]{\mathrm{eps}} \, \frac{\|\boldsymbol{u}\| + 1}{\|\boldsymbol{v}\|}
```
with the displacement $\boldsymbol{u}$ and the Jacobian-vector product vector $\boldsymbol{v}$.
The user parameter can be used to scale the perturbation, but is set to `1.0` as default.
This now drastically improved the convergence in many simulations.

The ZEM scaled somehow with the grid, which was related to the $\omega_0$ parameter that according to Silling should be calculated as
```math
\omega_0(\boldsymbol{X}) = \int_{\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{X})} \omega(\boldsymbol{\Delta X}) \, \mathrm{d}V' \quad .
```

title: Removed possible deadlock in job processing
body:
It is now possible to call `process_each_job` inside a `@mpiroot` call.
Previously, if an error occurs during processing, a deadlock will happen because the error handling attempts an MPI barrier, but non-root ranks are not participating in the `process_each_job` call at all.
This is now fixed, of `only_root=true` is used.

```julia
# Correct: Use only_root=true when inside @mpiroot
@mpiroot :wait begin
    results = process_each_job(study, default; only_root=true) do job, setup
        # ... processing code
    end
end

# Incorrect: This will deadlock on errors
@mpiroot :wait begin
    results = process_each_job(study, default) do job, setup  # Missing only_root=true
        # ... processing code
    end
end
```

title: Process each export with result collection
body:
## Enhanced `process_each_export` with Result Collection

This PR adds optional result collection functionality to `process_each_export`, inspired by the design of `process_each_job`. Users can now easily collect and combine data from processing multiple export files without writing intermediate files.

**Optional Result Collection**
- Add `default_value` parameter to enable collecting results into a vector
- Maintains 100% backward compatibility (legacy mode when `default_value=nothing`)
- Works seamlessly with serial, multithreaded, and MPI backends

**MPI Support**
- Distributed processing with `MPI.Allgatherv` for parallel mode
- Proper broadcasting with `MPI.Bcast!` for serial mode
- All ranks receive identical complete results
- Type safety validation (`isbitstype` requirement)

### Usage Example

```julia
# Collect statistics from all export files
default_value = (; max_disp=NaN, avg_ux=NaN)
results = process_each_export(job, default_value) do r0, r, id
    max_disp = maximum(r[:displacement])
    ux = @view r[:displacement][1, :]
    avg_ux = sum(ux) / length(ux)
    return (; max_disp, avg_ux)
end
# results is Vector{NamedTuple} with one entry per export file
```

title: Custom export fields
body:
It is now possible to specify a new custom field by defining two methods:
```julia
# necessary for the field checker, if the user specified fields are available
custom_field(::Val{:my_field}) = true

# 
function export_field(::Val{:my_field}, mat, system, storage, paramsetup, t)
    # maybe some calculations on `my_field`
    return storage.my_field
end
```
This makes it possible that some properties that are not necessary for the force density calculation are calculated only during the time steps that they are actually exported and written to disk.
Doing it this way, it saves computational time and makes it possible to calculate custom fields.
For the `BBMaterial`, `DHBBMaterial` and `OSBMaterial` this feature is now used to calculate the `:strain_energy_density`, for the `CMaterial` and `CRMateiral`, it is used to calculate `:von_mises_stress`.

This feature is only internal API.

```julia
# new feature:
mat = BBMaterial() # the same as below
mat = BBMaterial(dmgmodel=CriticalStretch())

# implementation now easily possible (but not implemented yet)
mat = BBMaterial(dmgmodel=CriticalEnergy())
mat = BBMaterial(dmgmodel=CriticalStress())
```

title: Add flexible boundary condition handling via matrix
body:
This PR introduces a more flexible method for applying boundary conditions using a matrix.

This approach is particularly beneficial for complex scenarios where the boundary condition values cannot be directly expressed as a function of time or location. Examples include values derived from experimental data or results from other solvers. In this method, each row of the matrix corresponds to a specific dimension, while each column maps to a position of a PD node. By assigning values to the appropriate elements in the matrix, it is possible to define boundary conditions for individual PD nodes. Furthermore, by implementing a function to update the matrix dynamically during each iteration, this method allows for seamless adjustment of boundary values at every time step. This capability is especially useful in cases where boundary conditions evolve dynamically, such as in fluid-structure interaction simulations.

Key changes:

    Introduced a matrix to represent boundary conditions.

Benefits:

    Provides greater flexibility and adaptability for handling diverse and dynamic boundary conditions.
    Enables easy integration of experimental or solver-based boundary values.
    Facilitates precise control over individual PD nodes, ensuring compatibility with a wide range of scenarios.

Verification:

 Velocity boundary condition validation: The new boundary condition method has been validated by comparing it with quasi-static results from a tensile test in https://kaipartmann.github.io/Peridynamics.jl/stable/generated/tutorial_tension_static/#tutorial_tension_static. The results are consistent with the theoretical predictions. Below is the input file used for the validation.
```
using Peridynamics
inp_file = joinpath(@__DIR__, "TensileTestMesh.inp")
body = Body(BBMaterial(), inp_file)
point_sets(body)

# Declare the dimensions involved in boundary conditions. 
# 1 represents the x-direction, and 2, 3 represent the yz directions. 
# If all three dimensions are involved, dims = UInt8[1, 2, 3].
dims = UInt8[1]

# Define a matrix to describe the boundary conditions. 
# The number of rows is equal to the number of dimensions, 
# and the columns are initialized for all points.
v_matrix = zeros(length(dims), length(body.point_sets[:all_points]))

# Assign values to the boundary points in the matrix according to the boundary conditions.
for i in body.point_sets[:all_points]
    if i ∈ body.point_sets[:bottom]
        v_matrix[1, i] = -0.6  # Set boundary condition for the bottom
    elseif i ∈ body.point_sets[:top]
        v_matrix[1, i] = 0.6   # Set boundary condition for the top
    end
end

material!(body; horizon=0.01, rho=2700, E=70e9, Gc=100)
velocity_bc!(v_matrix, body, :bottom, dims)
velocity_bc!(v_matrix, body, :top, dims)

vv = VelocityVerlet(steps=500)
job = Job(body, vv; freq = 1, path="results/tension_dynamic_fracture_vbc", fields=(:velocity_half, :damage))
submit(job)
```
Force boundary condition validation: 
The force boundary condition was validated using a 3D block model, where the left end was fixed and a tensile force was applied at the right end. This simulation follows Fig 8.14 on page 161 of the reference book “Peridynamic Theory and Its Applications“. The results align with the theoretical solution and are consistent with the findings from the literature. Below is the input file used for this test.
```
using Peridynamics
l, w, h, Δx = 1.0, 0.1, 0.1, 1/100
pos, vol = uniform_box(l+3Δx, w, h, Δx; center=(-1.5Δx, 0, 0))
body = Body(BBMaterial{EnergySurfaceCorrection}(), pos, vol)
point_set!(p -> p[1] <-l/2, body, :left)
point_set!(p -> p[1] > l/2-Δx, body, :right)

# Declare the dimensions involved in boundary conditions. 
# 1 represents the x-direction, and 2, 3 represent the yz directions. 
# If all three dimensions are involved, dims = UInt8[1, 2, 3].
dims_f = UInt8[1]
dims_v = UInt8[1, 2, 3]

# Define a matrix to describe the boundary conditions. 
# The number of rows is equal to the number of dimensions, 
# and the columns are initialized for all points.
f_matrix = zeros(length(dims_f), body.n_points)
v_matrix = zeros(length(dims_v), body.n_points)

# Assign values to the boundary points in the matrix according to the boundary conditions.
for i in body.point_sets[:all_points]
    if i ∈ body.point_sets[:right]
        f_matrix[1, i] = 2e10 # Set boundary condition for loading in y direction
    elseif i ∈ body.point_sets[:left]
        v_matrix[:, i] .= 0.0 # Set boundary condition for fix layer
    end
end

material!(body; horizon=3.015Δx, rho=7850.0, E=200e9, epsilon_c=1.0)
velocity_bc!(v_matrix, body, :left, dims_v)
forcedensity_bc!(f_matrix, body, :right, dims_f)

vv = DynamicRelaxation(steps=30000)
job = Job(body, vv; freq = 500, path="results/tensile_vbc", fields=(:displacement, :b_ext))
A = submit(job)
```

```julia
using Peridynamics

function sphere_impact(; ns=6, np=3, path)
    Ø = 0.15
    ΔX0_sphere = Ø / ns
    pos_sphere, vol_sphere = uniform_sphere(Ø, ΔX0_sphere; center_z=Ø / 2 + ΔX0_sphere)
    sphere = Body(BBMaterial{EnergySurfaceCorrection}(), pos_sphere, vol_sphere)
    failure_permit!(sphere, false)
    material!(sphere; horizon=3.1ΔX0_sphere, E=210e9, rho=8000, Gc=2000)
    velocity_ic!(sphere, :all_points, :z, -20)
    lxy, lz = 2.0, 0.1
    ΔX0_plate = lz / np
    pos_plate, vol_plate = uniform_box(lxy, lxy, lz, ΔX0_plate; center_z=-lz / 2)
    plate = Body(BBMaterial{EnergySurfaceCorrection}(), pos_plate, vol_plate)
    material!(plate; horizon=3.1ΔX0_plate, E=27e9, rho=2700, Gc=10)
    ms = MultibodySetup(:sphere => sphere, :plate => plate)
    contact!(ms, :sphere, :plate; radius=min(ΔX0_sphere, ΔX0_plate))
    vv = VelocityVerlet(steps=2000)
    job = Job(ms, vv; path=path)
    @time submit(job)
    return nothing
end

##
path = "results/benchmarks/sphere_impact"
rm(path; recursive=true, force=true)
sphere_impact(; path) # compilation
sphere_impact(; ns=20, np=8, path) # work
```

Due to the Polyester-Threads mixing issue I thought it could be a good idea to also use `Polyester.@batch`, so it is used for every multithreading loop in the package in `v0.3.0`:
```julia
## Peridynamics.jl v0.3.0 - everywhere using Polyester.@batch
# compilation:
# 89.256836 seconds (47.14 M allocations: 14.914 GiB, 0.66% gc time, 7.14% compilation time)
# work:
# 45.514108 seconds (40.16 M allocations: 128.786 GiB, 8.94% gc time)
```

However, I found out this was the reason my parallel performance for single body simulations is not as good as before. When changing all `Polyester.@batch` statements in `Peridynamics.jl` to `@threads :static` calls, the performance of contact simulations also improves (if `PointNeighbors.jl` also uses `@threads :static`):
```julia
## Peridynamics.jl v0.3.1-DEV - everywhere using Threads.@threads :static
## PointNeighbors.jl v0.4.5: update_grid!(...; parallelization_backend=ThreadsStaticBackend())
# compilation:
# 106.717161 seconds (54.34 M allocations: 15.806 GiB, 0.61% gc time, 5.13% compilation time)
# work:
# 39.184317 seconds (48.59 M allocations: 129.752 GiB, 9.53% gc time)
```
